title: The Fork
subtitle: One piece, two threats
summary: A fork is any single move that attacks two targets at once, so the defender can only save one. This study centers on the classic knight fork of a king and queen, then shows the same idea worked by a pawn and by a queen — forks are a geometry, not a piece.

rootAnnotations.title: A fork is geometry, not a piece
rootAnnotations.body: A fork just means one move attacks two undefended (or under-defended) targets at the same time. Knights are famous for it because their attack pattern is so unusual, but any piece can fork — a pawn attacks two squares diagonally at once, and a queen can hit two targets down two different lines from a single square.

rootAnnotations.title: Scan for pieces that are undefended and reachable together
rootAnnotations.body: Before you look for a fork, look at what the opponent has left loose. Here, Black's queen on c8 and both rooks on d6 and f6 are undefended — nobody is guarding them. That alone is the invitation. The next question is always the same: is there one square from which I attack two of these at once, and is that square itself safe?

annotations.title: No rush
annotations.body: The fork isn't going anywhere, so White plays a spare move first. Notice what's already true of the position: the knight on d5, the queen on b2, and even the pawn on e4 all have a forking resource sitting one move away — see the variations on this move for the pawn's and the queen's versions of the same idea.

White's knight is on d5 and Black's king and queen are on g8 and c8. Is there a single knight move that gives check to the king and attacks the queen in the same instant? Find the square before reading on.

annotations.title: The royal fork
annotations.body: From e7, the knight attacks g8 — check — and c8, where the queen sits, at the same moment. Nothing about Black's position lets both problems be solved with one move; a king in check must be dealt with immediately, and moving the king does nothing to save the queen.

annotations.title: Forcing moves make forks unbreakable
annotations.body: This fork happens to come with check, which is what makes it completely safe. An ordinary double attack sometimes lets the opponent create a bigger threat of their own and ignore it. A check removes that option entirely — the only legal replies address the king, and none of Black's king moves touches c8.

annotations.title: Why the knight is untouchable here
annotations.body: Check that e7 isn't attacked by anything black before playing this: no pawn, rook, or the king can capture the knight. That's the other half of what makes knight forks so strong — a knight's attack pattern lets it land on squares that a queen or rook fork could never safely use, because nothing moves the way a knight does. Compare this to the queen's fork in the variation below, which has to work much harder to find a safe square.

annotations.title: Pawns fork too
annotations.body: The pawn on e4 advances to e5, and now attacks d6 and f6 diagonally — both rooks — at once. This is the exact same relationship as the knight fork: one move, two undefended targets, only one of which can be saved. Nobody thinks of a pawn push as a tactic, which is exactly why it catches people off guard.

annotations.title: Only one rook escapes
annotations.body: Black saves the d6-rook. There is no move that rescues both — the f6-rook is simply lost.

annotations.title: A whole rook, for free
annotations.body: The least valuable piece on the board just won a full rook. That's the real lesson of the pawn fork: the fork's strength comes from the geometry of the attack, not from the value of the piece making it.

annotations.title: A queen fork — but it has to earn its safety
annotations.body: The queen jumps from b2 to e5, attacking d6 and f6 along two different diagonals — a genuine fork. Unlike the knight, though, the queen had to find a square that neither rook could capture along a rank or file, since rooks move in straight lines. e5 works because the attack on each rook comes diagonally, a direction no rook can answer.

annotations.title: The same choice as before
annotations.body: Again Black can only save one rook. The mechanism is identical to the pawn fork — what changes is which piece is doing the forking, and how carefully that piece had to check its own safety first.

annotations.title: Cashing in
annotations.body: The queen collects the second rook cleanly. Three different pieces — knight, pawn, and queen — just executed the same idea on the same board. That is the whole point: learn to see the relationship, not a specific piece's trick.

annotations.title: Every flight square loses the queen
annotations.body: The king has more than one legal square to go to, but it doesn't matter which one it picks — none of them defends or blocks the knight's attack on c8. That's what makes this a true fork rather than a simple threat: the forcing half (check) and the material half (the hanging queen) are completely independent of each other.

annotations.title: Collecting the point
annotations.body: The knight was never in danger for a single move of this sequence — nothing black ever attacked e7, and now it simply takes the queen. That total safety, start to finish, is what a well-spotted fork looks like in practice.

annotations.title: Too late to matter
annotations.body: Black finally attacks the knight, but the damage is already done — White is up a full queen for a knight.

annotations.title: What you should have noticed
annotations.body: Before every move, glance at the opponent's undefended pieces and ask: is there one square that hits two of them? Checks and captures are the strongest forking vehicles because they're forcing — the opponent must answer them before doing anything else. And remember the knight's special trick: because it doesn't move in straight lines, it can often land on a forking square that a queen, rook, or pawn could never safely use — but as the variations showed, those other pieces fork constantly too, as long as they double-check their own landing square is safe.
